paragraphs.text: Gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina is an autosomal recessive chorioretinal degeneration associated with hyperornithinemia. It is caused by deficiency of ornithine-delta-aminotransferase (OAT), an enzyme of the mitochondrial matrix (Mitchell et al., 1988). The disorder is characterized by progressive constriction of the visual fields, a 10- to 20-fold elevation in plasma ornithine, and reduced activity of L-ornithine:2-oxoacid aminotransferase. Atrophy of type II muscle fibers is morphologically conspicuous but clinically unimportant, and it progresses along with the eye disease (Sipilä et al., 1981). Vision declines in early life, eventually leading to complete blindness (Balfoort et al., 2021).

paragraphs.text: Kaiser-Kupfer et al. (1983) described cataract in 9 phakic patients with gyrate atrophy. They also examined 3 cataractous lenses removed from patients aged 31 to 47 years. Clinically, the lens opacities lay mainly along the confluence of the posterior sutures and interfered with vision because they were in the visual axis. Histologically, the posterior suture region was filled with liquified and degenerated lens material typical of senile cataractous changes. The authors concluded that by the second decade, cataract is a uniform finding in gyrate atrophy, and that it appears to be unique compared with the cataracts of other forms of retinal degeneration.

(1999) studied the central nervous system in 23 untreated patients with gyrate atrophy (mean age 32 +/- 18 years), comparing them with age-matched healthy controls and with 9 patients who had taken creatine or creatine precursor supplements for several years. The EEG findings were not associated with the MRI changes or with the patients' age or sex.

paragraphs.text: Peltola et al. (2002) looked for peripheral nervous system involvement in 40 patients with gyrate atrophy (mean age 31.6 +/- 16.3 years; range, 5 to 74 years). Neurography was abnormal in 21 patients (53%), and the abnormalities were associated with the severity of the ophthalmologic changes and with age. Quantitative sensory threshold testing showed abnormal large-fiber function in 7 patients (18%) and abnormal small-fiber function in 4 (10%). Somatosensory and brainstem auditory evoked potential responses were abolished in 5 patients. The authors concluded that gyrate atrophy is a systemic disease that affects the peripheral as well as the central nervous system.

paragraphs.text: Balfoort et al. (2021) carried out a systematic review of 33 studies covering 107 patients; there were no randomized controlled trials or large cohort studies. Treatments included protein-restricted diets, pyridoxine supplementation, creatine or creatine precursor supplementation, L-lysine supplementation, and proline supplementation. paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (1988) studied 4 Lebanese patients with gyrate atrophy from 2 pedigrees. Using grep, I searched for zygosity, ancestry and variant details. The only specific mutation is the initiator-codon ATG-to-ATA change in Mitchell et al. (1988). That abstract does not say whether the 4 Lebanese patients were homozygous, nor does it give a protein-level name. Brody et al. (1992) report 21 new alleles but do not specify any in the abstract. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so I gave no gene MIM number; I took the chromosome location 10q26 from Barrett et al. (1987). The zygosity in the intro rests on the 'bi-allelic' statement in Balfoort et al. (2021).
